advances: The original product of finite log-concave nonnegative height laws of mean one admits independent latent labels such that every conditional height row has mean one and every conditional centered linear height sum has fourth moment at most 236844 times its squared variance. The labels can be attached by Bayes' rule to arbitrary original transverse kernels, preserving the entire original joint product law and the conditional centering of the transverse noise. This supplies a regular latent scalar center without requiring equal transverse means across components.
author: research-agent
proof:
Apply the exact decomposition theorem of accepted fact `889f821f12f55878` separately to each \(p_i\). Its scalar variable \(X\) is the present \(Y_i\), its integral mean \(j\) is 1, its component count \(L\) is the present \(R_i\), and its component parameter \(s_\ell\) is \(\log q_{i,\ell}\). That accepted theorem gives an equality of the original masses, positive weights, and component means exactly one. A nonsingleton component has integral support endpoints \(a<1<b\) inside the original nonnegative support. Hence \(a=0\) and \(b=B\ge2\). A singleton component is \(\delta_1\). This proves the representation and the asserted support form. Although that predecessor already provides a stronger component fourth-moment bound, we verify the stated elementary constants directly.

Fix a nondegenerate component and temporarily omit its row and label indices. For \(q>0\), let \(Z_B(q)=\sum_{y=0}^B q^y\) and let \(F_B(q)=\sum_{y=0}^B yq^y/Z_B(q)\). Differentiating these finite sums gives \(qF_B'(q)=\operatorname{Var}_{B,q}Y>0\), because both 0 and 1 have positive masses. Thus the mean is strictly increasing in \(q\). If \(B=2\), the equation \(F_2(q)=1\) is \(q+2q^2=1+q+q^2\), so \(q^2=1\) and the positive ratio is \(q=1\). This is the uniform law on \(\{0,1,2\}\).

Suppose \(B\ge3\). At \(q=1/2\), the finite component is a nonnegative geometric random variable of mean one conditioned to be at most \(B\). The conditioning event and its complement both have positive probability, and every value on the complement exceeds every value on the event. Its conditional mean is therefore strictly below the unconditional mean, so \(F_B(1/2)<1\). For fixed \(q>0\), adding the support point \(B+1\) strictly increases the finite mean: that point exceeds every point already in the support. At \(q=2/3\) direct finite summation gives
\[
 Z_3(2/3)=\frac{65}{27},
 \qquad \sum_{y=0}^3 y(2/3)^y=\frac{66}{27},
 \qquad F_B(2/3)\ge F_3(2/3)=\frac{66}{65}>1.
\]
Strict monotonicity and \(F_B(q)=1\) now imply \(1/2<q<2/3\), including existence and uniqueness of the ratio for each such \(B\).

For \(0<q<1\), let \(G_q\) have the untruncated geometric masses \((1-q)q^y\), \(y\ge0\), and put \(\mu=q/(1-q)\). The component just considered is exactly the law of \(G_q\) conditional on \(G_q\le B\). The same ordering between this event and its complement, applied to the increasing function \(y^4\), gives \(\mathbb E Y^4\le\mathbb E G_q^4\). To calculate this last moment exactly, differentiating the convergent geometric series \(t\) times and multiplying by \((1-q)q^t\) gives \(\mathbb E (G_q)_t=t!\mu^t\) for \(1\le t\le4\), where \((y)_t=y(y-1)\cdots(y-t+1)\) is the falling factorial. Using \(y^4=(y)_4+6(y)_3+7(y)_2+(y)_1\),
\[
 \mathbb E G_q^4
 =24\mu^4+36\mu^3+14\mu^2+\mu
 \le24\cdot16+36\cdot8+14\cdot4+2
 =730,
\]
because \(q<2/3\) gives \(0<\mu<2\), and every coefficient is positive. This proves the raw fourth-moment bound for \(B\ge3\). For every nonnegative integer \(y\), \((y-1)^4\le y^4+1\): at \(y=0\) both sides equal one, and at \(y\ge1\) the inequality follows from \(0\le y-1\le y\). Hence \(\mathbb E(Y-1)^4\le731\).

Also \(Z_B(q)\le\sum_{y=0}^{\infty}q^y=1/(1-q)\le3\). Consequently the component masses satisfy \(\nu_0=1/Z_B(q)\ge1/3\) and \(\nu_1=q/Z_B(q)\ge1/6\). If \(Y'\) is an independent copy of \(Y\), the identity \(\operatorname{Var}Y=\mathbb E(Y-Y')^2/2\) shows, just from the two ordered pairs \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\), that \(\operatorname{Var}Y\ge\nu_0\nu_1\ge1/18\). Thus
\[
 \mathbb E(Y-1)^4
 \le731
 \le731\cdot18^2(\operatorname{Var}Y)^2
 =236844(\operatorname{Var}Y)^2.
\]
For the \(B=2\) uniform component, its raw fourth moment is \(17/3\), its variance is \(2/3\), and its centered fourth moment is \(2/3\). The standardized centered fourth moment is therefore \(3/2\), which is below \(K_0\); the two absolute moment bounds hold as well. For \(\delta_1\), the raw fourth moment is one, and both centered moments and the variance are zero. This proves every component bound, including the degenerate case.

Now fix any label tuple in the product construction. Its probability is positive, because the weights are positive. Under its conditional law the variables \(T_i=c_i(Y_i-1)\) are independent and centered. Put \(v_i=\mathbb E[T_i^2\mid\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_k]\). Scaling the component inequality by \(c_i^4\) gives \(\mathbb E[T_i^4\mid\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_k]\le K_0v_i^2\), also for \(c_i=0\) or deterministic heights. Independence and centering eliminate every term in the fourth-power expansion with an index appearing exactly once. Hence, with all expectations in the next display conditional on the fixed tuple,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E W&=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}W=\sum_i v_i,\\
 \mathbb E W^4
 &=\sum_i\mathbb E T_i^4+6\sum_{i<h}v_iv_h\\
 &\le K_0\sum_i v_i^2+2K_0\sum_{i<h}v_iv_h
 =K_0\left(\sum_i v_i\right)^2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here \(K_0\ge3\) justifies \(6\le2K_0\). If all \(v_i=0\), the centered sum is zero almost surely, so the assertion still holds with both sides zero. Summing over labels gives the original height product, since the one-row height masses sum to \(p_{i,y}\), and both the independent label draws and the conditional height draws factor across rows.

Finally attach the labels to the given original joint product. At every height of positive original mass, the displayed Bayes probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one by the exact mixture identity. Because they depend only on \(y\), they define a label draw conditionally independent of \(\mathbf X_i\) given \(Y_i=y\). Multiplying the original mass-kernel expression \(p_{i,y}K_{i,y}(A)\) by that probability proves the joint identity in the statement. If \(p_{i,y}=0\), nonnegativity of the mixture terms and positivity of all weights imply \(\nu^{(i,\ell)}_y=0\) for every \(\ell\); such heights have no probability and need no Bayes denominator or conditional kernel choice.

Summing the joint identity first over \(y\) and taking \(A=\mathbb R^{r_i}\) gives \(\Pr(\Lambda_i=\ell)=\pi_{i,\ell}\). Dividing by that positive weight gives the conditional row law \(\nu^{(i,\ell)}_yK_{i,y}(A)\). Summing instead over \(\ell\) gives the original row law \(p_{i,y}K_{i,y}(A)\). The original independent rows and conditionally independent label draws have joint product law
\[
 \Pr(\mathbf X_i\in A_i,Y_i=y_i,\Lambda_i=\ell_i\text{ for all }i)
 =\prod_i\pi_{i,\ell_i}\nu^{(i,\ell_i)}_{y_i}K_{i,y_i}(A_i).
\]
This proves independence of the labels, independence of the rows conditional on their labels, preservation of every original kernel, and preservation of the original joint product marginal. In particular the earlier conditional height-sum proof applies to exactly this coupling.

The assumed integrability and the finite height supports make every \(\mathbf m_i(y)\) and every \(N_i\) integrable. Conditional on \(Y_i=y,\Lambda_i=\ell\) with positive probability, the unchanged kernel gives \(\mathbb E\mathbf X_i=\mathbf m_i(y)\). Therefore \(\mathbb E[N_i\mid Y_i,\Lambda_i]=0\). The joint product formula shows that conditioning on all heights and labels leaves the transverse coordinates with independent kernels \(K_{i,y_i}\), so each corresponding conditional row noise expectation is zero, and summing proves the stated expectation for \(N\).

Integrating the conditional row law gives \(\mathbb E[\mathbf X_i\mid\Lambda_i=\ell]=\sum_y\nu^{(i,\ell)}_y\mathbf m_i(y)\). The scalar equation \(\sum_y y\nu^{(i,\ell)}_y=1\) imposes no equality between these transverse vectors. Likewise, averaging the conditional fourth-moment inequality gives an upper bound by \(K_0\mathbb E[(\operatorname{Var}(W\mid\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_k))^2]\), rather than by the square of the unconditional variance. The proof requires neither of the excluded assertions.
statement:
Let \(k\ge1\). For each \(1\le i\le k\), let \(p_i=(p_{i,y})_{y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}}\) be a probability law with finite contiguous positive support \(\{M_i,\ldots,N_i\}\), with its zero extension satisfying \(p_{i,y}^2\ge p_{i,y-1}p_{i,y+1}\), and with \(\sum_y yp_{i,y}=1\). There exist positive weights \(\pi_{i,\ell}\), \(1\le\ell\le R_i\), summing to one, and laws \(\nu^{(i,\ell)}\), supported inside the original height support, such that
\[
 p_{i,y}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{R_i}\pi_{i,\ell}\nu^{(i,\ell)}_y,
 \qquad \mathbb E_{\nu^{(i,\ell)}}Y_i=1.
\]
Each component is either \(\delta_1\), or has, for an integer \(B_{i,\ell}\ge2\) and a finite positive ratio \(q_{i,\ell}\), masses
\[
 \nu^{(i,\ell)}_y
 =\frac{q_{i,\ell}^{y}}{\sum_{z=0}^{B_{i,\ell}}q_{i,\ell}^{z}}
 \quad(0\le y\le B_{i,\ell}),
 \qquad \nu^{(i,\ell)}_y=0\quad\text{otherwise}.
\]
If \(B_{i,\ell}=2\), then \(q_{i,\ell}=1\) and the component is uniform on \(\{0,1,2\}\). If \(B_{i,\ell}\ge3\), then \(1/2<q_{i,\ell}<2/3\). Every component satisfies
\[
 \mathbb E Y_i^4\le730,
 \qquad \mathbb E(Y_i-1)^4\le731,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E(Y_i-1)^4\le K_0(\operatorname{Var}Y_i)^2,
 \qquad K_0=236844,
\]
where the expectations and variance in this display are under that component. For every nondegenerate component with \(B_{i,\ell}\ge3\), also \(\nu^{(i,\ell)}_0\ge1/3\), \(\nu^{(i,\ell)}_1\ge1/6\), and \(\operatorname{Var}Y_i\ge1/18\).

Sample labels \(\Lambda_i\) independently with \(\Pr(\Lambda_i=\ell)=\pi_{i,\ell}\), and conditional on all labels sample heights independently with laws \(\nu^{(i,\Lambda_i)}\). The unconditional height law is exactly \(\bigotimes_i p_i\). For all real \(c_1,\ldots,c_k\), put \(W=\sum_i c_i(Y_i-1)\). For every label tuple,
\[
 \mathbb E[W\mid\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_k]=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E[W^4\mid\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_k]
 \le K_0\bigl(\operatorname{Var}(W\mid\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_k)\bigr)^2.
\]
This includes zero coefficients and zero conditional variance.

More generally, for each \(i\), let \(r_i\ge1\), and let the original pair \((\mathbf X_i,Y_i)\), with \(\mathbf X_i\in\mathbb R^{r_i}\), have height marginal \(p_i\) and any prescribed conditional kernel \(K_{i,y}\) for \(\mathbf X_i\) given \(Y_i=y\). Assume \(\mathbb E\|\mathbf X_i\|<\infty\), and take the original pairs independently. Define \(\mathbf m_i(y)=\int\mathbf x\,K_{i,y}(d\mathbf x)\) at each height of positive original mass. The labels above can be attached to these original pairs by the conditional probabilities
\[
 \Pr(\Lambda_i=\ell\mid\mathbf X_i,Y_i=y)
 =\frac{\pi_{i,\ell}\nu^{(i,\ell)}_y}{p_{i,y}}
 \qquad(p_{i,y}>0),
\]
using conditionally independent label draws across rows. This coupling has the same independent label law, the same conditional product height laws, and
\[
 \Pr(\mathbf X_i\in A,Y_i=y,\Lambda_i=\ell)
 =\pi_{i,\ell}\nu^{(i,\ell)}_y K_{i,y}(A)
\]
for every measurable \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^{r_i}\). In particular, deleting the labels recovers exactly the original joint product law, and the kernel of \(\mathbf X_i\) given \(Y_i=y,\Lambda_i=\ell\) is the unchanged \(K_{i,y}\) whenever that event has positive probability.

For arbitrary vectors \(\mathbf u_i\in\mathbb R^{r_i}\), define the row noises \(N_i=\mathbf u_i\cdot(\mathbf X_i-\mathbf m_i(Y_i))\) and their sum \(N=\sum_iN_i\). This coupling satisfies
\[
 \mathbb E[N_i\mid Y_i,\Lambda_i]=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E[N\mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_k,\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_k]=0.
\]
Only the scalar height means are common to the components: the conditional transverse mean at label \(\ell\) is \(\sum_y\nu^{(i,\ell)}_y\mathbf m_i(y)\), which is not required to equal the original transverse mean. The fourth-moment assertion is conditional on the labels, and makes no unconditional standardized fourth-moment assertion for \(W\) or directional regularity assertion for the full transverse-height blocks.
